assets.title: The Spreadsheet That Beat Ads
assets.body:
My first 40 customers came from a spreadsheet — not ads.

I opened a blank sheet. Listed 200 companies that had publicly complained about the exact problem I was solving. Sent 200 emails. Each one quoted their own words back to them.

No ad spend. No generic templates. Just proof I'd actually read their complaint.

That's how you get your first 40 customers with zero budget and zero audience.
rationale: Score of 78 with a concrete, visual mechanic (spreadsheet, 200 emails) — this is a payoff you show, not explain, which is exactly what Shorts reward.
Fits Alex's direct/practical tone with zero motivational fluff — just the literal method.
Self-contained in 38s, no setup needed from other moments.

assets.title: I Tripled My Price And Lost Zero Customers
assets.body:
I tripled my price and lost exactly zero customers.

Here's what nobody tells you about pricing early: your first ten customers aren't buying software. They're buying a fix for a problem that's already costing them more than your price tag.

If your price feels safe, it's probably too low.
rationale: Score 78 and a single quotable stat that lands in one breath — ideal Short structure, no thread needed to make the point.
Reframes a founder pricing fear directly and practically, matching Alex's educational tone without hype.
Routed to Shorts over LinkedIn per suggested list because the payoff is a punchline, not a framework to unpack.

assets.title: Why My Cold Emails Got A 19% Reply Rate
assets.body:
My cold email reply rate was 19%.

That's absurd for cold outreach — because it wasn't actually cold.

Every email quoted the exact words the recipient had used to complain about the problem I solved.

Personalization isn't a subject-line trick. It's proof you did the reading.
rationale: This moment is the 'why' behind the spreadsheet Short — it's analytical, not visual, so it reads better as a tight X post than a second Short covering similar ground.
Score 78, and the counterintuitive stat (19%) is a strong standalone hook for X's scroll pace.
Keeps the insight distinct from the first 40 customers Short to avoid duplicating the same beat across formats.

assets.title: Why A Low Starting Price Signals 'Toy'
assets.body:
1/ I started my SaaS at $19/month because that felt safe.

It wasn't safe. It signaled the product was a toy.

2/ Low prices don't just cost you revenue — they cost you credibility. Early customers read your price as a signal of how seriously you take your own product.

3/ When I moved to $59, the conversation changed. People stopped asking 'is this free?' and started asking about onboarding.

Price is positioning before it's revenue.
rationale: This is a framework-shaped insight (price as signal, not just revenue) — per routing rules that belongs in a thread, not a Short, so the reasoning has room to land.
Folds in the follow-on moment (price change conversation shift) as the thread's payoff line rather than forcing a second overlapping asset.
Score 78/75 across both source moments supports a confident but not inflated 76.

assets.title: The Question That Changed When I Raised My Price
assets.body:
When I raised my price from $19 to $59, something shifted.

People stopped asking if it was free. They started asking about onboarding.

Same product. Different price. Completely different buyer mindset.
rationale: Score 75 is solid but the moment is thin standalone — most of its value already lives in the thread asset, so confidence is held at 68 rather than inflated.
Included as an optional standalone post for creators who want to run it separately from the thread, but flagged lower since it risks feeling redundant if published alongside the thread.

assets.title: The Footer That Quietly Drove A Third Of My Signups
assets.body:
One of the highest-leverage things I built into my SaaS wasn't a feature — it was a footer.

Every customer's output — the thing they created and shared with their own audience or team — carried a small footer linking back to the product.

By week four, that footer was responsible for roughly a third of new signups.

No ad spend. No growth hacking gimmicks. Just a distribution channel built into the product's natural use.

If your product produces something shareable — a report, a graphic, a document — you already have a growth loop. You just haven't labeled it yet.

Worth asking: what does your product create that someone else will see?
rationale: Lowest score of the set (68) and the mechanism needs explanation to land — a newsletter gives room to unpack the loop instead of compressing it into a punchline, which a Short or single X post can't do justice.
Structural, not visual — routed by payoff per the mandate rather than following the suggested-platform habit list.
Confidence held at 68, matching the original score, since the '1/3 of signups' claim needs the reader to trust the setup, not just the number.
